messages.content: My kitchen breaker trips whenever the microwave and the toaster run at the same time. Each one is fine alone. Is the breaker going bad?

Almost certainly not — the breaker is doing its job, and the arithmetic shows why. Read the wattage labels: a typical microwave draws about 1,200 W and a toaster about 900 W. Together that is 2,100 W. On a 120 V circuit, current is watts divided by volts: 2,100 / 120 = 17.5 A. If those outlets sit on a 15 A breaker, you are asking for 17.5 A through a device whose whole purpose is to open the circuit above 15 A. It trips after a short delay because 17.5 A is a mild overload, not a short.

The safe fixes are behavioral or structural, never a bigger breaker. Run the two appliances one at a time, or move one of them to an outlet on a different circuit (verify it is a different circuit by flipping breakers and testing, not by guessing from the room). Swapping in a 20 A breaker on wiring sized for 15 A is the one move you must never make: the breaker protects the wire in the wall, and oversizing it lets the wire become the fuse. If you want both running at once, an electrician can add a dedicated circuit — that is the real fix.
A breaker in my panel looks weird — the handle is stuck halfway between on and off, and pushing it toward on does nothing. The bedroom lights are out. What is happening?

That halfway handle is the tripped position. Breakers are designed to move there when they open on a fault or overload, so you can spot the tripped one at a glance — it is the one that does not line up with the others.

The reset sequence matters: push the handle firmly all the way to OFF first. You should feel it click past the middle. That re-arms the mechanism. Then push it to ON. If you only wiggle it from the middle toward ON, it never actually resets, which is the most common reason people conclude a breaker is broken.

Before you reset, unplug or switch off what was running in the bedroom when the lights died, so you are not resetting straight back into the same overload. If the breaker trips again immediately, or trips repeatedly over the next day, stop resetting it — an instant re-trip means a short circuit or a failing appliance, and that is an electrician's job, not a reset-and-hope job.
Every outlet in my bathroom stopped working, but no breaker in the panel is tripped and the lights still work. Where do I even look?

Look for a GFCI outlet — the kind with the small TEST and RESET buttons between the sockets. Bathroom outlets are wired in a chain, and one GFCI protects every outlet downstream of it. When it trips, the whole chain goes dead even though the breaker never moved, and the lights survive because they are usually on a separate circuit.

The tricky part is that the GFCI itself may not be in the bathroom that lost power. Builders often feed two bathrooms, a garage outlet, or an outdoor outlet from one GFCI, so check every bathroom, the garage, and any outlet near the kitchen sink. A tripped GFCI shows a popped RESET button and sometimes a small amber light.

Unplug everything from the dead outlets first, then press RESET. If it clicks and holds, plug things back in one at a time — the hair dryer or a damp appliance may be what tripped it. If RESET will not stay in, or it trips again with nothing plugged in, that points to moisture or a wiring fault, and it is time for an electrician rather than repeated resets.
My garage GFCI trips the instant I reset it, even with nothing plugged in anywhere on that circuit. I have reset it maybe ten times today. What should I do?

Stop resetting it — that is the first and most important step. A GFCI that trips instantly with no load is telling you one of two things: there is a real ground fault somewhere on the circuit (current leaking where it should not, often through moisture in an outdoor outlet box or damaged insulation), or the GFCI device itself has failed, which they do with age. Ten resets do not distinguish between those, and each reset re-energizes a fault you cannot see.

What you can safely do is observe and narrow down. Check every outdoor and garage outlet on that circuit for water in the box, cracked covers, or a cover left open in rain. Note whether the tripping started after rain, pressure washing, or sprinkler work — that timing is valuable information. Look, but do not open boxes or touch wiring.

Then call an electrician and hand over exactly what you observed: trips instantly, no load, started after whatever event. A failed GFCI is a cheap replacement; a ground fault in a buried or outdoor run is the thing you want found by someone with insulation testers, not by trial and error at the reset button.
A breaker trips two or three times a week, always at odd hours, and the refrigerator is on that circuit. How do I figure out whether it is the fridge or just bad luck?

Intermittent trips are a logging problem before they are an electrical problem. Start a simple log: date, time, what else was running, and whether the fridge was humming when you found it. Refrigerators draw a heavy surge when the compressor starts and a smaller extra load during the automatic defrost cycle, which runs on a timer — often at odd hours, which matches your pattern.

Do the load arithmetic for the whole circuit, not just the fridge. A fridge averages 100–200 W running but the circuit may also carry a microwave, a coffee maker, or counter outlets. If the summed steady loads sit near the breaker rating, the compressor's start surge can be the straw that trips it — an overload pattern. If the circuit is lightly loaded and trips still land randomly, suspicion shifts to the appliance or a failing breaker.

One safe experiment: run an extension lead from the fridge to an outlet on a different circuit for a few days (a heavy-duty cord, routed where it cannot be pinched). If the trips follow the fridge, the appliance is the culprit and a refrigerator technician is next. If the trips stay with the old circuit, call an electrician. Either way, your log is what turns a vague complaint into a diagnosis.
There is a faint burning smell near my electrical panel and I am not sure if I am imagining it. Nothing has tripped. Should I open the panel and look?

Do not open the panel. A burning smell at the panel is one of the clear stop-and-call signs in a house: it can mean a loose connection heating up, a breaker failing internally, or insulation breaking down — all of them inside a box you should never open, because the service conductors in there stay live even with every breaker off.

Here is your safe sequence. Trust your nose; a new electrical burning smell (sharp, like hot plastic or fishy in older insulation) that localizes to the panel is real until a professional says otherwise. Do not reset, flip, or exercise breakers to test it. If you see sparking, smoke, or hear sizzling, leave the area and call emergency services from outside, then your utility. If it is smell only, call an electrician today — this is a same-day call, not a next-week call — and mention 'burning smell at panel, nothing tripped' exactly; they will triage it as urgent.

While you wait, reduce load on the house if you can do it from the appliance side (unplug the space heater, hold off on the dryer), and keep people and pets out of the room with the panel. The observation you already made — smell, location, no trip — is the complete homeowner contribution here. The rest belongs to someone with the training and the insulated tools.
My new space heater trips the bedroom breaker after about twenty minutes. The heater says 1500 watts. The breaker is 15 amps. Is that combination just doomed?

Do the division: 1,500 W / 120 V = 12.5 A. That is under 15 A, so why the trip after twenty minutes? Two reasons stack up. First, electrical code treats a load running for hours as continuous and sizes it at 80 percent — a 15 A circuit is really a 12 A circuit for continuous loads, and your heater alone is 12.5 A. Second, the bedroom circuit is never carrying only the heater: lights, a TV, phone chargers, and a clock add up, and breakers are thermal devices — a modest overload takes minutes to heat the trip mechanism, which is exactly your twenty-minute delay.

Practical options, all safe: run the heater on its low setting (often 750 W, about 6.3 A) and see if the trips stop — that also confirms the diagnosis. Or move the heater to a circuit with little else on it, ideally a 20 A circuit, plugged directly into the wall outlet, never through an extension cord or power strip. If it trips a lightly loaded 20 A circuit on low, the heater itself is faulty and goes back to the store.

What not to do: swap the breaker for a larger one. The breaker is matched to the wire in the wall, and the wire does not care that you are cold.
How do I tell whether dead outlets mean a tripped GFCI or a tripped breaker? I keep checking the wrong thing first.

Use the pattern of what died; the house tells you which device acted.

If the lights in the room still work and only a cluster of outlets is dead — especially outlets in bathrooms, the kitchen, the garage, or outdoors — think GFCI. Those outlets are chained behind one GFCI device, and it trips silently without touching the breaker. Go hunting for the outlet with TEST and RESET buttons, remembering it may live in a different room from the dead outlets.

If a whole room or a whole zone went dark — lights and outlets together — think breaker. Go to the panel and look for the handle sitting in the middle position, out of line with the rest.

Two refinements. If some outlets in a room work and others do not, that split usually means the room spans two circuits or a GFCI chain covers only part of it — map which outlets died and the pattern will name the protector. And if nothing in the entire house works, that is neither: check whether the neighbors are dark too, and call the utility. Pattern first, panel second — you will check the right thing first almost every time.
The breaker for my air conditioner trips right when the unit tries to start, maybe once a week. The AC runs fine the rest of the time. Can I just keep resetting it?

You can reset it once to restore cooling, but treat the pattern as a symptom to be diagnosed, not a routine. A compressor draws several times its running current for a fraction of a second at startup. A healthy breaker tolerates that surge because its trip curve allows brief overcurrents. A breaker that trips at startup once a week is telling you the margin is shrinking — the compressor may be starting harder as it ages (a weak start capacitor is the classic cause), or the breaker itself is weakening from heat cycles.

Your homeowner-scope work is observation: log which trips happen at startup versus mid-run, note the outdoor temperature (the hardest starts happen on the hottest afternoons, when head pressure is highest), and check that the outdoor unit's airflow is not choked by shrubs or a clogged coil — you can look, and you can hose dust off the outside of the coil with the power off at the disconnect only if you are comfortable; when in doubt, skip it.

Do not keep resetting a breaker that starts tripping more often, and never hold a breaker closed or upsize it. Book an HVAC technician and hand them your log: 'trips at startup, weekly, worse on hot days' points them straight at the capacitor and compressor health instead of a generic inspection.
Half the labels on my breaker panel are wrong or faded. What is the safe way to build a correct breaker map?

This is one of the highest-value afternoons you can spend on a house, and it is entirely observation work. You need two people, two phones, a plug-in radio or lamp, and a marker.

One person stands at the panel; the other walks the house. Flip one breaker off. The walker checks every room: which lights died, and — using the lamp or a phone charger plugged in turn — which outlets died. The radio trick speeds this up for outlets: plug it in loud, and the person at the panel flips breakers until the music stops. Call out findings, write them down, then move to the next breaker. Kitchens and bathrooms need outlet-by-outlet care because they often mix two circuits and a GFCI chain.

Record more than the room: note the breaker's amperage from its handle (15 or 20), and flag the special ones — the double-width breakers for the range, dryer, water heater, and AC. Photograph the finished map and keep a copy in the house log and one on your phone.

Do this on a calm weekend, warn everyone in the house, and save work on computers first — you will cut power to everything once. The next time something trips at midnight, the map turns a flashlight panic into a thirty-second lookup.
My arc-fault breaker trips whenever I run the vacuum cleaner, but nothing else trips it. Is the breaker defective?

Probably not defective — this is a known personality clash. An AFCI breaker listens for the electrical signature of arcing: the ragged, spiky current draw of a sparking connection. A vacuum cleaner's universal motor makes sparks on purpose at its brushes, and to the breaker that can look uncomfortably like the real thing. Older AFCIs are especially prone to this nuisance tripping.

Distinguish nuisance from warning before you dismiss it. Nuisance pattern: trips only with the vacuum (or a treadmill, or an old drill), only on that circuit, and the appliance's cord and plug are clean and undamaged. Warning pattern: trips with many different loads, trips with nothing running, or you find a cord with nicks, a plug that runs warm, or a burnt smell anywhere on the circuit — that is the breaker catching a genuine arc, and it goes to an electrician, not to the ignore list.

A safe test: run the same vacuum on a different AFCI circuit. If it trips that one too, the vacuum's signature is the problem — vacuum on a non-AFCI circuit where code allows, or replace the aging vacuum. If only the one breaker objects to everything, the breaker or the circuit wiring needs a professional look. Never swap an AFCI for a plain breaker to silence it; the protection exists because bedroom wiring faults start fires quietly.
My 1875-watt hair dryer kills the bathroom power every single morning. The outlet is a GFCI and I reset it, but it happens again the next day. What is going on?

Start with the dryer's own number: 1,875 W / 120 V = 15.6 A. That single appliance exceeds a 15 A circuit by itself, before the lights, a curling iron warming up, or anything else joins in. If your bathroom circuit is 15 A, the dryer is simply too big for it on high — and the trip may be happening at the breaker, not the GFCI, even though you notice it at the outlet. Check the panel next time before resetting anything: if a breaker handle sits mid-position, that is your answer.

Modern codes put bathrooms on 20 A circuits precisely because dryers grew to this size; a 20 A circuit carries 15.6 A comfortably. So the diagnosis splits by what you find. Breaker tripping on a 15 A circuit: overload, expected, and the fixes are running the dryer on medium (often about 1,000 W, roughly 8.3 A), drying in a room on a 20 A circuit, or having an electrician add a proper 20 A bathroom circuit. GFCI tripping with the breaker untouched, especially if the dryer is old or has been dropped in the sink area: the dryer may be leaking current, and the GFCI is protecting you — retire the dryer.

Either way, the daily reset is the symptom log, not the solution. Identify which device trips first; they are telling different stories.
One breaker in my panel feels slightly warm and I think I hear a faint buzzing from the panel at night. Everything works fine. Can this wait until my next day off?

No — put it on the short list, as in call an electrician this week and say the words 'warm breaker and buzzing' when you book. Here is why the combination matters. A breaker carrying a heavy load can feel faintly warm; that alone is common. Buzzing is different: it suggests a connection that is not tight — a breaker not fully seated on the bus bar or a loose terminal — and loose connections arc microscopically, which makes heat, which loosens things further. It is a slow spiral that ends in a scorched breaker or worse, and it does all this while everything in the house works fine.

Your part is senses only: note which breaker (count down from the top, note its label), whether the warmth and buzz track with a big load running (dryer, AC, oven), and whether you ever catch a hot-plastic smell. Do not press on the breaker to seat it, do not open the panel, and do not ignore a buzz that gets louder or a smell that appears — those escalate the call to same-day.

The fix, when the electrician comes, is usually unglamorous: reseat or replace the breaker, torque the terminal, inspect the bus for heat damage. Cheap now, expensive after it cooks. Warm plus buzzing plus working fine is exactly what early warning looks like — the house is being polite about it.
When my dryer starts, the lights flicker. Sometimes it is just the laundry room, sometimes the whole house seems to dip. How do I tell whether this is my problem or the power company's?

The flicker's footprint is the diagnostic. A dryer motor's startup surge pulls a brief, heavy current, and voltage dips a little wherever that current shares a path. Localize by watching which lights dip.

If only laundry-room lights dip, the surge is traveling a single branch circuit — the lights and dryer share wiring, and the dip is normal physics, worth a note but rarely a fault. If every light in the house dips together, the shared path is your whole service: the main feed is sagging under the surge, which can mean an undersized or aging service, or a deteriorating connection at the meter or panel — an electrician or the utility needs to find which side of the meter it lives on.

One pattern changes the urgency completely: if some lights get BRIGHTER while others dim, stop diagnosing and call the utility and an electrician promptly. Brightening is the signature of a failing neutral connection, which can swing voltage far above and below normal and cook electronics throughout the house. Dimming is a sag; brightening is an imbalance, and imbalance is dangerous.

Cheap confirming observation: ask a neighbor on the same transformer whether their lights dip when your dryer starts (coordinate by phone). If theirs dip too, the transformer or utility feed is undersized — that is squarely the power company's problem, and your call to them can say exactly that.
The GFCI on my patio will not reset after last night's rainstorm. It was fine yesterday. Do I need a new one?

Maybe, but let the weather finish testifying first. Outdoor outlet boxes collect water: wind drives rain past the cover, condensation forms inside, and a GFCI only needs a few thousandths of an amp leaking through that moisture to trip — and to refuse reset while things stay wet. A GFCI that worked yesterday and fails the morning after a storm is most often wet, not dead.

Safe sequence: unplug anything connected out there. Look at the box without opening it — is the weather cover cracked, hanging open, or the wrong type (a flat cover protects nothing while a cord is plugged in; the bubble-style in-use cover does)? Then wait for a full dry day and try the reset again. If it resets and holds once everything is dry, moisture was the fault, and the lasting fix is a sound in-use cover — and an electrician if the box itself needs resealing or replacement.

If it still will not reset after two dry days, or it trips again in dry weather with nothing plugged in, the device has likely failed or there is a genuine fault downstream. That is an electrician visit. Do not defeat the GFCI by swapping in a plain outlet outdoors — the location is exactly why the protection exists, and the next wet morning would find the fault with no one listening.
Is there a difference between a breaker that trips the instant I reset it and one that trips ten minutes later? Both keep happening on my garage circuit.

Yes — the timing is the diagnosis, and your garage circuit is showing you both chapters.

An instant trip, the moment the handle reaches ON, means the current is enormous the instant power returns: a short circuit (hot touching neutral or ground) or a dead-shorted appliance still plugged in. The breaker is not being picky; it is interrupting a fault that would otherwise be an arc flash in a wall. Never keep forcing resets against an instant trip. Unplug everything on the circuit and try once: if it holds with nothing connected, plug items back in one at a time and the instant trip will name the guilty appliance. If it trips instantly with the circuit empty, the fault is in the wiring itself — electrician, full stop.

A delayed trip, minutes later, is the thermal signature of an overload: current modestly above rating, heating the breaker's trip element until it lets go. Ten minutes at 18 A on a 15 A breaker is textbook. The cure is load arithmetic and redistribution, not parts.

Garage circuits earn both: a freezer, a power tool, and a space heater conspire into overloads, while a nicked cord or a rodent-chewed run in a wall provides the short. Timing first, then the plug-by-plug test, then the phone call — in that order.
I run my space heater through a long extension cord so I can put it across the room. The cord gets warm. Is that normal or a problem?

It is a problem, and the warmth is the warning label. A 1,500 W heater draws 12.5 A continuously. Light extension cords are often rated 10–13 A when new and perfect; coiled, kinked, run under a rug, or just long, they shed heat badly and their resistance climbs. Warmth at the cord means electrical energy is being spent heating your floor instead of the room, and plug connections are the hottest points of all — that is where cords melt and fires start.

The voltage-drop side is quieter damage: a long thin cord can drop several volts, so the heater underperforms while its plug and the cord ends run hot. People respond by buying a bigger heater, which makes every number worse.

The rule is simple and absolute: space heaters plug directly into a wall outlet, full stop — manufacturers print it on the tag for exactly this reason. If the warm spot in the room is far from an outlet, move the chair, not the heater's tether. If you truly need heat at that spot permanently, an electrician adding an outlet is the safe version of the idea. And retire that warm cord from heater duty entirely; heat-cycled insulation does not recover.
The printed directory inside my panel door says things like 'plugs' and 'lights' with no rooms named. Why does everyone say a good breaker map matters so much?

Because every electrical problem you will ever troubleshoot starts with the same question — what else is on this circuit? — and a good map answers it in seconds instead of an hour of flipping and shouting.

Consider the three moments it pays off. A breaker trips at night: the map tells you instantly whether the dead fridge shares a circuit with the countertop outlets (an overload story) or sits alone (an appliance story). A GFCI hunt: the map notes which outlet hosts the GFCI for a chain, so you stop checking the wrong rooms. A pro visit: the electrician bills by the hour, and 'the fault is somewhere in the house' is a much more expensive sentence than 'it is the 15 A circuit feeding the garage and patio, here is what is on it.'

Building it is pure observation — two people, a lamp or radio, one breaker at a time, writing down lights and outlets separately for each room, plus the amperage on each handle and the big double breakers for range, dryer, water heater, and AC. Date it, photograph it, keep it in the house log.

The vague directory you have now is what builders leave; the map is what owners make. It is the difference between the house being a black box and the house being a system you can reason about — which is the entire game in home diagnosis.
One lamp in my living room flickers. Everything else in the room is steady. Where is the fault most likely to be?

A flicker that lives in exactly one lamp almost never comes from the house wiring — it localizes to the lamp, its bulb, or the single outlet feeding it, because a circuit fault would take its neighbors flickering with it. Work the ladder of cheap swaps.

First, swap the bulb with a known-good one from a steady lamp. LED bulbs flicker as their internal drivers fail, and a loose screw-base contact does it too — power off at the switch, reseat the bulb firmly. Second, move the lamp to a different outlet on a different wall. If the flicker follows the lamp, the lamp is guilty: check its cord for pinch damage and its switch for a loose, crackly feel; lamp switches and sockets wear out and are the classic source. If the flicker stays with the original outlet while a different lamp behaves there, suspect the outlet's grip on the plug — try wiggling nothing, just note whether the plug sits loosely.

Third, the boundary case: if the lamp flickers only when something big elsewhere starts (AC, washer), that is not this problem — that is a shared-circuit dip. A one-lamp flicker that survives a new bulb, a different outlet, and a cord inspection earns an electrician only if the outlet itself is implicated; loose outlet connections heat up quietly. But nine times out of ten, the bulb or the lamp switch confesses by the second swap.
All the lights in my den pulse brighter and dimmer in a rhythm whenever the washing machine is running in the next room. Steady otherwise. Should I worry?

A rhythmic pulse synced to the washer's cycle is one of the more legible flickers: the washer's motor starts and stops repeatedly as it agitates, and each start pulls a surge that sags the voltage briefly. If the den lights share the washer's circuit — common when a laundry area was carved out of a room's wiring — they ride every sag. The rhythm matching the agitation cycle is the fingerprint that separates this from random flicker.

Confirm with observation, no tools opened up: does the pulsing stop during the washer's fill and drain phases and return during agitation and spin-up? Does a light in a far room stay steady? If yes to both, you have a shared-circuit load interaction — annoying, usually benign, and fixable properly only by giving the washer its own circuit (an electrician job, and code expects laundry circuits to be dedicated for this reason).

Worry instead if the pattern changes character: pulsing with nothing running, some lights flaring brighter than normal while others dim, or flicker spreading to rooms that never flickered. Brighter-than-normal is the loose-neutral signature and jumps the queue to an urgent call. Rhythm tied to one appliance, steady elsewhere, nothing ever brighter — that is a load story, and you can schedule it rather than fear it.
Something odd: when the AC kicks on, half my lights get dimmer but the kitchen lights actually get brighter. My neighbor said that is bad. Is it?

Your neighbor is right, and this is one of the few flicker patterns that deserves the word urgent. Dimming under a heavy load is a plain voltage sag. Brightening is different physics: it is the signature of a failing neutral connection.

Here is the picture. Your service delivers two 120 V legs balanced around a neutral. With a healthy neutral, each leg holds near 120 V. When the neutral connection deteriorates — at the meter, the panel, or the utility's drop — the two legs unbalance: a heavy load on one leg (your AC) drags that leg's voltage down and pushes the other leg's voltage UP. Lights on the loaded leg dim; lights on the other leg get over-voltage and flare brighter. That over-voltage side can swing far enough to destroy electronics, motors, and power supplies anywhere on that leg, and the bad connection itself is heating.

So: stop troubleshooting, do not wait for it to get worse, and make two calls — your utility (a failing neutral is often on their side, at the service drop, and they treat these as priority) and an electrician if the utility clears their side. Unplug sensitive electronics until it is fixed. This is not a someday item and not a DIY item; it is the house showing you a fault that damages things while you watch. Brightening lights are never a quirk — they are an alarm.
One outlet in my bedroom is dead. The others work. Give me the order of things to check before I call anyone.

Work from the protectors inward, cheapest checks first.

One: is it really just the outlet? Plug in a lamp or charger you have just seen working elsewhere. A dead phone charger impersonates a dead outlet every day.

Two: look for a GFCI upstream. Bedrooms are not usually on GFCI chains, but bathrooms, garages, and outdoor outlets are — and additions sometimes tie rooms together oddly. If any GFCI in the house is tripped, reset it and retest.

Three: the panel. Look for a breaker handle in the middle position. If the whole circuit were down, the room's other outlets would likely be dead too — but if this bedroom's outlets split across two circuits, one tripped breaker can kill exactly the outlets on one wall.

Four: the half-hot possibility. Try the wall switch by the door with something plugged in — many bedrooms have one outlet (often just the top socket, and often installed upside down as a hint) controlled by the switch for a lamp.

If all four come up empty — known-good device, no tripped GFCI, no tripped breaker, no switch control — the fault is at the outlet or its connections, which is where homeowner scope ends. Loose back-stabbed connections are the usual cause, and replacing or re-terminating an outlet is electrician territory for most people. Your four checks just saved you paying a call-out fee for a wall switch.
I noticed the outlet behind my toaster oven feels warm to the touch, and the plug is warm too. It works fine though. How concerned should I be?

Warm is a stop sign — treat this outlet as out of service until an electrician has seen it. Here is the reasoning. A healthy outlet and plug carrying a load should feel essentially neutral. Warmth means resistance somewhere in the connection: worn contacts gripping the plug blades poorly, a loose terminal, or a plug whose blades are tarnished or bent. Resistance under load becomes heat, heat degrades the contact further, and the cycle escalates quietly behind a wall plate. This is precisely how electrical fires start — not with a bang, but with a warm outlet someone meant to mention someday.

Stop using that outlet today, and unplug by gripping the plug body, not the cord. Look without touching anything internal: is there discoloration on the plate, a brown tinge, a faint hot smell? Note it for the electrician. Move the toaster oven to another outlet and watch whether that plug also warms — if it does, the appliance's plug itself is the resistor and the oven's cord needs replacing; if not, the original outlet is the fault.

Do not open the outlet, do not bend plug blades to grip tighter, and do not decide it is fine because it still works. Faults like this work fine right up until they do not. Warm outlet plus warm plug is the house asking politely, once.
Plugs keep falling out of my living room outlets, or hanging half out. It is annoying but is it actually a problem worth fixing?

It is a genuine problem, not just an annoyance — a plug hanging half out is an electrical fault in slow motion. Inside the outlet, spring contacts are supposed to grip the blades firmly. After decades of use they fatigue and relax. A loose grip means a tiny contact area carrying the full load, which arcs microscopically and heats; and a half-seated plug leaves live blade metal exposed where a child's hand, a pet's nose, or a fallen metal object can bridge it.

Notice the pattern to report: is it every outlet in the room (same age, same wear — a whole-room replacement conversation) or one abused outlet under the TV? Does any plug feel warm after running a load, or do you see dark marks on blades? Warmth or scorch marks promote this from 'schedule it' to 'stop using that outlet now.'

The fix is outlet replacement, which means working on wiring inside the box — for most homeowners this is an electrician line item, and a cheap one since they can do a room in a single visit. Do not try to fix grip by bending plug blades outward; that stresses the blade and worsens the contact geometry. And skip the plastic plug-in 'tighteners' — they mask the wear without restoring contact pressure.

Until the visit: move loads that run unattended (heaters, chargers overnight) to sound outlets, and leave the loosest ones empty. Worn outlets are one of the best-value fixes in an older house — small money, real fire risk retired.
My hallway light is controlled by two switches. After a handyman replaced one switch, the light only comes on when both switches are up. It used to work from either switch. What did he do?

He almost certainly landed a traveler wire on the wrong terminal. Here is the logic so you can verify the diagnosis by behavior. A three-way setup has two switches connected by two 'traveler' wires, plus one common wire on each switch — on the first switch the common brings power in, on the second the common feeds the light. Flipping either switch reconnects the path through one traveler or the other, which is why either switch can always change the light's state: four switch combinations, light on in two, off in two, and any single flip toggles it.

Your symptom — on only when both are up — means one switch's common and a traveler got swapped. The circuit now completes only for one specific combination, and the other three are dead. That truth table is the tell: proper three-way behavior toggles from any flip; yours requires a magic combination.

The good news: nothing is dangerous in the usual case, and the diagnosis is complete from the behavior alone. The fix is swapping two wires on one switch's terminals — inside-the-box work, so it goes back to the handyman (his callback, his cost) or an electrician. Tell them 'common and traveler are swapped on the replaced switch; light only works with both up.' You will sound like you know three-way wiring cold — because now you do. Do not let anyone 'fix' it by replacing the other switch too; the fault is in the one that was touched, and in home diagnosis the last thing changed is suspect number one.
I swapped my dining room bulbs for LEDs and now the dimmer buzzes and the lights shimmer at low settings. The old incandescents were fine. Bad bulbs?

More likely a compatibility problem than bad bulbs. Your old dimmer was built for incandescents: it chops the AC waveform (leading-edge dimming), and a filament smooths that out by glowing through the gaps. An LED has electronics inside — a driver — that expects a clean waveform and tries to regulate against the chopped one. The argument between them produces exactly your symptoms: buzz at the dimmer (its components vibrating under the chopped load), shimmer and flicker at low settings (the driver starving and restarting), and sometimes a pop-on effect where nothing happens until the slider is a third up, then full brightness.

Test before you spend: put one bulb from a different brand in — driver designs vary and some tolerate older dimmers well. Check the bulb box for 'dimmable' (non-dimmable LEDs on a dimmer will always misbehave) and check the dimmer maker's compatibility list online, which names tested bulbs.

The durable fix is pairing parts from this decade: a modern LED-rated dimmer (trailing-edge) matched to dimmable bulbs. Replacing a dimmer switch is in-wall wiring — an electrician for most homeowners, though it is a quick visit. The buzz alone is the sound of a mismatch, not an emergency; but a dimmer that also runs hot to the touch stops being a compatibility story and becomes a stop-using-it story. Note which it is before you call.
One recessed light in my kitchen keeps turning itself off after about half an hour, then comes back on later. The bulb is not burned out. Ghosts?

Not ghosts — a thermal protector doing its job. Recessed cans have a temperature switch that cuts power when the fixture gets too hot and restores it as things cool, which produces your exact cycle: on for a while, off, back on later. The question is why it runs hot.

Work the likely causes in order of probability. First, the bulb: a higher-wattage bulb than the can is rated for, or an LED whose driver cooks in an enclosed can — read the fixture's rating label (visible inside the can with the bulb out and power off at the switch) and compare it with the bulb you installed. Second, insulation: cans not rated for insulation contact (non-IC) overheat when attic insulation is piled over them; if this started after insulation work, that timing is the confession. Third, a failing thermal switch itself — possible, but diagnose the heat first.

Your safe checks are all with the switch off: bulb wattage versus the printed rating, and whether other cans on the same run stay on (they should — heat is local to this fixture). If the bulb matches the rating and it still cycles, or the can is buried in insulation, that is an electrician conversation — the protector is a messenger, and defeating it or ignoring it converts a warning into a fire risk above your ceiling. The light is not haunted; it is hot, and it is telling you so in the only language it has.
Half of one outlet in my bedroom never works — the bottom socket is fine, the top one is dead. Is the outlet broken?

Probably not broken — you have likely found a switched outlet, a deliberate feature. In rooms without ceiling lights, builders wire one outlet so a wall switch controls it for a lamp. Often only half the duplex is switched: the top socket answers to the switch while the bottom stays live always. Many installers even mount the switched outlet upside down as a quiet signal to future owners.

Test it in ten seconds: plug a lamp into the top socket, leave the lamp's own switch on, and flip the wall switch by the door. If the lamp obeys the wall switch, the outlet is healthy and you have gained a feature — that top socket is exactly where a bedside or reading lamp belongs.

If the wall switch does nothing and the top socket stays dead with a known-good lamp, then yes, something is wrong at that outlet — a failed socket or a loose connection — and it joins the electrician list. But run the switch test first. A remarkable number of 'dead outlets' in bedrooms, living rooms, and dens are switched halves doing their job for owners who never got told. And note it on your breaker map and house log, so the next person in this house skips the mystery entirely.
There is a buzzing sound coming from a wall switch in my hallway. The light works. I only hear it in the evening when the house is quiet.

A buzzing switch is not a wait-and-see item, even with the light working. Switches are supposed to be silent. Buzzing means something inside is vibrating at line frequency — classically a loose connection or a failing contact that is arcing in tiny bursts as current crosses a poor joint. Each arc pits the contact further, so buzzes like this do not heal; they ripen. The evening detail fits: you hear it when the house is quiet, and the hallway light is on for long stretches then, heating the marginal connection.

Your scope is ears and nose only. Does the switch plate feel warm? Is there a faint hot or sweet chemical smell near it? Does the buzz change when you flip the switch off and on? Note the answers, then stop using that switch if you can route around it — leave the light off — and book an electrician, mentioning 'buzzing switch, works, no smell' or whatever you found; if you found warmth or smell, say so and treat it as urgent.

Do not remove the plate to look. The fault you are imagining is exactly the kind that lives behind it. The likely repair is a switch replacement — minutes of work for a pro — but the diagnosis you deliver ('buzz started recently, only under load, plate cool') is what gets it triaged right. A silent switch is a healthy switch; one that talks to you is asking for help.
When the microwave runs, the lights in the dining room dim noticeably — but the microwave is in the kitchen. Different rooms, so does that mean they share a circuit?

Not necessarily the same branch circuit — but they share something, and the dimming depth tells you how much. A microwave pulls roughly 1,200–1,500 W, about 10–12.5 A, and that current flows through every conductor upstream of it: its branch circuit, the panel bus, and the service feed. Voltage drops a little across each shared segment. A slight, barely-there dip in another room is the service feed's small resistance — normal, seen in most houses.

A noticeable dim in a different room deserves one more observation: is it only the dining room, or does the whole house breathe with the microwave? Only one other room suggests the two rooms' circuits may actually be tied together somewhere — older homes accumulate creative wiring, and kitchen remodels borrow circuits. Whole-house dimming points at the service: an aging or long service drop, or connections at the meter loosening with heat cycles.

Use your breaker map (or build it now — this question is a perfect excuse): find the microwave's breaker and the dining lights' breaker. Different breakers plus strong dimming means the shared segment is upstream, which is utility-or-panel territory. Then the deciding observation: do any lights anywhere get brighter while the microwave runs? Brighter means a failing neutral, and that converts this from curiosity to urgent — call the utility and an electrician. Dimming alone, moderate and stable for years, is a characteristic of your service; dimming that is new or worsening is a connection going bad somewhere, and that trend is the thing to report.
My porch light works fine in winter but in summer it often will not come on at dusk, or it comes on very late. It has a light sensor. What changes with the season?

The photocell itself is the prime suspect, and the season is the clue that convicts it. A dusk-to-dawn sensor switches when light falls below a threshold. In summer, dusk arrives late and slowly, and the sensor — aging, its little window clouded or dirty — hovers near its threshold in bright twilight and may never quite decide it is dark, or decides an hour late. In winter, darkness falls fast and deep, far past the threshold, so even a tired sensor trips decisively. Marginal components fail at margins, and summer dusk is the margin.

Two other seasonal actors to rule out by observation. Heat: a sensor or LED driver baking in a sun-struck fixture all afternoon can misbehave until it cools — note whether failures follow the hottest days. Light pollution from the fixture itself: if the sensor can 'see' the bulb it controls or a neighbor's new bright light, it may think dawn never ended; check what the sensor faces.

Safe checks: wipe the sensor window clean (dirt films cost more light than people expect), and on a failing evening, cover the sensor fully with opaque tape for a minute — a healthy sensor turns the light on in the dark you made. If taped darkness works, the sensor is marginal and the fixture or sensor head needs replacing — fixture wiring, so electrician or a confident handyperson working with the breaker off; when in doubt, the pro. If taped darkness fails too, power or the fixture itself is at fault and the same call applies.
Two rooms lost power to their outlets at the same time. I checked the panel twice — no breaker is tripped. Lights in both rooms work. I am out of ideas.

You have checked the breaker; the other protector is still hiding. Outlets dead in two rooms with lights alive and no tripped breaker is the classic signature of a tripped GFCI feeding a chain that crosses room boundaries. The chain often starts somewhere you would never guess: the GFCI in a garage, a basement, an outdoor box, or the far bathroom can be the head of a line that wanders through both of your dead rooms — a wiring economy from the era when one GFCI protected everything downstream.

Hunt systematically: every outlet with TEST and RESET buttons in the house — bathrooms, kitchen, garage, basement, laundry, outdoors, even behind the refrigerator's neighbor or inside a bathroom cabinet. Press RESET on any that looks popped. The one that restores both rooms was your invisible breaker.

If a full sweep finds no tripped GFCI, widen once more: some houses have a GFCI breaker in the panel that looks almost like a normal breaker — check for a small test button on the breakers themselves, and re-check handles by touch, since a tripped handle can sit only slightly out of line. Feel each handle for the one that is springy rather than firm (with dry hands, touching only the handles — that is normal panel use).

Still nothing? Then the chain has a failed device or a broken connection, and the electrician gets a very useful brief: 'outlets dead in two rooms, lights fine, no breaker or GFCI tripped anywhere.' You have already done the diagnosis; you are paying for hands now, not for thinking.
My smart bulbs flicker, but only when I dim them below about twenty percent in the app. At full brightness they are perfect. The fixtures have no dimmer switch — just a normal switch. Why?

This one is the bulb's own electronics hitting their floor, not your wiring. A smart bulb dims by driving its LEDs with rapidly pulsed current from its internal driver. At moderate levels the driver has plenty to work with; near the bottom of the range it approaches the minimum current at which it can regulate stably, and below that floor it hunts — brightening, starving, restarting — which your eye reads as flicker and shimmer. Full brightness is perfect because the driver is in its comfort zone. The pattern 'only below twenty percent, only these bulbs' is the signature: a house wiring fault would not respect an app percentage.

Confirm by comparison: if you have two bulbs of the same model, both should flicker at roughly the same level; a different brand or model in the same fixture will usually have a different floor — some reach five percent cleanly. That swap test separates bulb behavior from fixture behavior without touching a wire.

Practical responses: set your scenes to stay above the flicker floor (twenty-five percent as the practical minimum), check the maker's app for a firmware update — minimum-dim behavior is exactly the kind of thing firmware improves — and when you buy more bulbs, treat the stated dimming range as a spec worth comparing. No electrician needed, and nothing here is a safety issue: it is a driver reaching the edge of its design, politely visible. The one change that would matter: if flicker ever appears at full brightness or spreads to ordinary bulbs in the same fixture, you are back in wiring territory — different symptom, different story.
Someone gave me a little plug-in outlet tester with three lights. What can it actually tell me, and what can it not?

That three-light tester is one of the best homeowner-scope tools there is — used within its limits. Plugged into an outlet, its light pattern reports the wiring basics: correct polarity (hot and neutral not swapped), presence of a ground connection, and the common mis-wirings — open ground, open neutral, open hot, hot/ground reversed. The legend printed on the tester decodes the patterns. It is perfect for surveying a new house, checking outlets after other work, and confirming an outlet is dead before you treat it as dead.

Now the limits, which matter just as much. It cannot tell you whether the ground is a GOOD ground — a bootleg ground (neutral jumpered to ground in the box) fools it completely and reads 'correct.' It cannot find a loose connection that only heats up under load, measure voltage, detect a shared neutral, or tell you which breaker feeds the outlet. And it tests at nearly zero load, so an outlet can pass and still misbehave with a real appliance.

The GFCI version of the tester adds a test button that should trip the GFCI protecting that outlet — a genuinely useful monthly check.

Use it as a screening instrument: a bad reading is real information and earns an electrician; a good reading means 'no obvious wiring error,' not 'certified safe.' For the price of a coffee it eliminates a whole family of guesses — just never let its three cheerful lights talk you into opening the box to fix what it found.
My toilet runs for a few seconds every so often, day and night, even when nobody has used it for hours. What is it doing?

It is refilling a slowly leaking tank. Inside the tank, the flapper — a rubber seal at the bottom — is supposed to hold the water until you flush. When the seal ages, warps, or gets grit under it, water seeps silently into the bowl. The tank level drops a fraction of an inch, the fill valve wakes up, tops it off, and goes quiet. Those few seconds of running, at random hours, are the sound of a leak measured in spoonfuls that adds up to hundreds of gallons a month.

Prove it with the dye test, the great zero-tool diagnostic: put several drops of food coloring in the tank, do not flush, and wait fifteen to twenty minutes. Color appearing in the bowl water means tank water is migrating past the flapper — confirmed leak. No color means the seal holds and you look instead at the fill valve or a water level set so high it spills down the overflow tube (look inside: the waterline should sit about an inch below the top of that tube, and there is often a marked line on the tank wall).

A flapper is one of the few genuinely homeowner-friendly plumbing parts — it unhooks and the new one hooks on, no tools, water off at the toilet's own shutoff valve first. Match the size (most are 2 inch, some 3). If the dye test is negative and the level is right yet the running continues, the fill valve is failing — still often a DIY swap, but a plumber is a fair call. Either way, the phantom running was never mysterious; it was arithmetic leaking.
My water bill crept up about thirty percent over two months and nothing in the house seems different. No puddles, no dripping faucets. Where is the water going?

Silent water loss has a usual suspect list, and one test rules the whole investigation: the meter test. Pick a time when nobody will use water for two hours (or overnight). Read the water meter and write down every digit, including the little leak-indicator dial if yours has one — on many meters a small triangle or star that spins with even tiny flow. Use no water at all in the window: no flushing, no ice maker cycles if you can help it, water heater idle. Read the meter again.

If the reading moved, water is leaving through something, full stop — you have proven a hidden leak exists before spending a minute finding it. The size of the move is your leak rate: say the meter advanced 6 gallons in 2 hours; that is 3 gallons an hour, 72 a day, over 2,100 a month — comfortably a thirty-percent bill surprise.

Then interrogate the usual suspects in order. Toilets first — statistically the champion: dye-test every toilet in the house (color in the tank, check the bowl in twenty minutes). Next, the water heater's T&P discharge pipe — is its end wet? Then irrigation lines and outdoor faucets, then a softener stuck in regeneration. If all come up clean and the meter still creeps, the leak is in a pipe you cannot see, and a plumber with acoustic detection earns their fee — hand them your two meter readings and the rate you computed. You will have turned 'the bill seems high' into 'we lose three gallons an hour,' and that is a diagnosis, not a complaint.
One bathroom faucet has weak pressure but every other faucet in the house is strong. The shower in the same bathroom is fine too. What is special about this one faucet?

When one fixture is weak and its neighbors are strong, the restriction lives in the last few inches of that fixture's path — and in a faucet, that means the aerator. The aerator is the little screen cap where the water exits; it traps sediment, mineral flakes, and grit precisely so they do not spray out, and over years it slowly strangles the flow. The shower being fine and the house pressure being fine eliminate everything upstream: the water arrives at that faucet under full pressure and then meets a clogged screen.

The fix is one of plumbing's genuinely homeowner-sized jobs: the aerator unscrews by hand or with a cloth-padded grip, you rinse the debris out of the screen (note how much grit there is — it is evidence about your water), soak it in vinegar if it is crusted with mineral scale, and screw it back. Pressure restored confirms the whole diagnosis retroactively.

If the aerator is clean and the faucet still dribbles, the next suspects are the faucet's own cartridge or the supply stop valves under the sink being partly closed — check that both angle stops are fully open by turning them gently counterclockwise. If one side only (hot or cold) is weak, that narrows it further to that side's stop or cartridge passage. But nine times out of ten, the screen is the story. One fixture weak, house strong: think local, think last-inch.
All the water pressure in my house dropped suddenly this morning. Every faucet, every shower, all weak. Nothing changed in the house. What do I check?

A sudden whole-house drop with no change inside the house points outward or at the single throat everything passes through. Check in this order.

First, the street test: ask a neighbor, or check whether there is utility work, a flushed hydrant, or a water-main repair on your street. A break or maintenance nearby drops a whole block, and if the neighbors are weak too, your job is done — it is the utility's, and they can usually tell you the restoration window.

Second, the main valve: if anyone recently touched the house's main shutoff or the meter (a plumber, a landscaper, the city reading the meter), a valve left half-closed strangles the whole house exactly like this. The main valve should be fully open — a gate valve turned fully counterclockwise, or a ball valve with its handle parallel to the pipe. Look, and if it is partway, open it fully; that is a homeowner move.

Third, the pressure-reducing valve (PRV): many houses have a bell-shaped PRV near the main, and when they fail they often fail toward low pressure. If the main is fully open, the neighbors are fine, and pressure is still uniformly weak, the PRV is the prime suspect — its replacement is plumber work, but your three observations just narrowed their visit to one part.

One caution: if the drop comes with discolored water, run a cold tap until it clears and do not drink it until it does — a main break stirs the system. Sudden, uniform, house-wide: think street, main valve, PRV — in that order, and you will rarely need step three.

The drain in my bathroom sink is slow, but the tub and toilet in the same bathroom drain fine. Meanwhile my sister says when HER drains are slow it is the whole house. How does the pattern tell us where the clog is?

Drainage is a tree, and the pattern of slow fixtures tells you which branch is blocked. Each fixture has its own small drain line; those join into branch lines, which join the house's main stack and sewer line. A clog slows everything upstream of it and nothing downstream or on other branches.

Your case: one slow sink, tub and toilet fine. The clog is in that sink's own short run — typically hair and soap sludge in the pop-up stopper and the trap right under the sink. It cannot be the main line, because the toilet moves far more water through that main and flushes clean. Your sister's case: everything slow, lowest fixtures worst, maybe gurgling — that pattern indicts the shared trunk, the main line, because every branch's water must pass it.

Use the tree logic as a map before touching anything: list which fixtures are slow and which are fine, and the clog sits just downstream of where the slow ones join and the fine ones do not. Two sinks on opposite sides of a wall slow together? Their shared branch. Only the kitchen slow after a big cooking day? The kitchen branch, probably grease.

For your sink: the stopper lifts or unclips out and usually brings the hair clog with it — that is homeowner scope, no chemicals needed (skip the caustic drain openers; they complicate any later plumber work and can damage older pipes). If water stands in several fixtures or the lowest drain in the house backs up, that is main-line territory — stop adding water and call a plumber, because the next flush has nowhere to go.
When I flush the toilet, the bathtub drain gurgles, and yesterday water actually came UP into the tub when the washer drained. Is this connected?

Completely connected, and the direction of travel is the alarm: water and air are being pushed back into your house instead of flowing out. Drains need two things — a clear path out and venting that lets air move. When the main line is partially blocked, a big discharge like the washer's pump-out cannot get through fast enough, so it pressurizes the line and escapes through the lowest, weakest openings it can find: the tub drain. Gurgling at the toilet flush is air being shoved through the tub's trap water on its way somewhere. Water rising in the tub is the same story one stage worse.

This pattern — multiple fixtures involved, symptoms at the LOWEST fixtures, flow reversing direction — is a main-line or septic problem, not a single-drain clog, and it is a stop-and-call situation for two reasons. First, the next stage is sewage backing up into the house, which is a health hazard and a miserable cleanup. Second, no homeowner tool reaches a main-line obstruction; it needs a plumber's auger or a camera, and possibly the city if the blockage is past your property line.

Until the plumber comes: minimize water use, do not run the washer or dishwasher, and flush sparingly. Tell them exactly what you told me — 'washer drain pushes water up into the tub, toilet flush gurgles the tub drain' — because that sentence alone tells them to bring main-line equipment and skip the small stuff. Your fixtures were talking to each other through the pipes, and what they were saying was: the exit is closing.
Ever since we got a new washing machine, the pipes bang loudly when it finishes filling. The old machine never did this. Coincidence?

Not a coincidence — that bang is water hammer, and your new machine is a faster door-slammer than the old one. The washer fills through solenoid valves that snap shut instantly. Water moving through the pipe has momentum; when the valve slams, the moving column stops dead and its energy becomes a pressure spike that races through the pipes and makes them jump and bang against their straps. Old machines used slower valves that eased shut, so the same plumbing never complained.

Why it matters beyond noise: those pressure spikes, repeated thousands of times, fatigue joints, loosen fittings, and shorten the life of supply hoses and appliance valves. The bang is the audible part of a real stress.

Diagnosis is already done by your observation — bang precisely at fill shutoff, only from the new machine, nowhere else in the house. Confirm once: run a sink faucet full blast and snap it off; a mild thud is normal, but the washer's bang should be distinctly worse, because its valve is faster and its flow is larger.

The remedies are plumber-scope but worth knowing so you can ask for them by name: water hammer arrestors fitted at the washer's supply valves (small sealed cylinders that cushion the spike), checking that pipe straps near the laundry are secure, and verifying the house's static pressure — if pressure is above about 80 psi, hammer gets violent and a pressure-reducing valve calms everything. Do not ignore a bang that starts cracking joints or coincides with a new drip at a fitting; then the stress has found a weak point, and the visit gets urgent.
My kitchen faucet drips. Sometimes from the spout, and lately I also see water around the base of the handle when I turn it off. Are these the same leak?

They are two different leaks with two different culprits, and where the water appears tells them apart — this is plumbing diagnosis at its most literal.

A drip from the spout, after the faucet is fully off, means water is getting past the valve's seal while closed. In a modern single-lever or cartridge faucet, the cartridge's seals have worn or grit has scored them; in an old two-handle compression faucet, the rubber washer at the stem's end has hardened. Either way the leak path is through the valve, and the drip rate tracks the failure — a drip every few seconds now becomes a stream of wasted water later. Note whether it is the hot side or cold side (feel the drip's temperature on a two-handle faucet): that names the guilty side.

Water appearing around the handle base or under the lever when you operate it is a different path: the packing or O-rings that seal the stem where it exits the faucet body. Those seals only get challenged when the stem moves or when the valve is pressurized in use, which is why this leak shows during operation rather than as an overnight drip.

Both are cartridge-and-seal problems inside the faucet — repairable, and for a confident homeowner a cartridge swap is a known DIY job with the water off at the sink's stops; for most people it is a quick plumber or handyman visit. Your contribution is the precise report: 'drips from the spout when off, hot side, about a drip every five seconds, plus seepage at the handle when closing.' A drip every five seconds, by the way, is roughly 17 drips a minute, around 900 gallons a year — the faucet is billing you for the diagnosis, so it is worth making.
My shower pressure fell off a cliff right after the plumber replaced a section of pipe in the basement. Before I call him back, is there anything obvious to check?

Yes — and the timing is your biggest clue. In home diagnosis, the last thing changed is suspect number one, and pipe work stirs up two classic after-effects.

First, debris. Cutting and soldering pipe knocks scale and sediment loose, and the first high-demand fixture used afterward collects it — which is usually the showerhead, whose tiny nozzles clog with grit. Unscrew the showerhead (hand-tight or a cloth-wrapped wrench), look at its inlet screen: if it is furred with flakes and grit, rinse it clean, run the shower pipe briefly without the head to flush the line, and refit. Pressure restored means the plumber's work was fine and physics just delivered the debris to you.

Second, a valve not fully reopened. Any shutoff that was closed for the repair — the shower's own stops if it has them, a zone valve, even the main — may have been left a quarter-turn short of open. Walk the path of valves the work touched and confirm each is fully open; a ball valve's handle should sit parallel to the pipe.

Check the rest of the house too: if only the shower suffered, it is debris at the head. If several fixtures weakened, it is a valve or debris at a shared point. Either way, when you call the plumber back you can say 'I cleared the showerhead screen and verified every valve you touched is fully open' — and if it is still weak, the remaining suspects (a kinked new section, solder blob restricting a joint) are his to find, armed with everything you ruled out.
My hot water used to last through two showers. Now the second shower goes lukewarm halfway through, and the water never seems as hot as it used to. The heater is electric, about nine years old.

An electric water heater has two elements and two thermostats, and your two symptoms point at the pair of them working as a team with one member down.

The upper element heats the top of the tank first — that is the water you draw first, and it is what makes the tap feel properly hot at the start. The lower element then reheats the bulk of the tank as cold water enters at the bottom. Now map your symptoms. 'Never as hot as it used to' plus 'runs out fast' most often means the LOWER element has failed: the upper still gives you an initially hot draw, but only the top slice of the tank is truly hot, so a long shower exhausts it quickly and the refill water below was never heated. The mirror-image failure — lower element fine, upper dead — gives the opposite signature: water that never gets hot at all, just endlessly lukewarm, because the upper thermostat never satisfies and never hands control down.

Your pattern fits lower-element failure, and nine years is a plausible age for it, especially with sediment insulating the bottom of the tank (listen for rumbling or popping during heating — sediment's voice).

Here is the boundary: elements and thermostats live behind covers with line voltage on their terminals. Testing them means a multimeter on live-adjacent components inside the heater — that is plumber or electrician work, not homeowner scope. What you hand over is the symptom story: 'initially hot, dies mid-second-shower, never reaches old temperature, nine years old, some rumbling.' That brief gets the right parts on the truck the first time.
The water from my hot taps came out rusty brown this morning after we were away for a week. Cold taps are clear. Should I be worried about my pipes?

The hot-only detail is the diagnosis: the color is coming from your water heater, not the house pipes. If the pipes themselves were rusting into the water, the cold side would show it too. After a week of sitting, the tank's water has had undisturbed contact with the tank's interior — and in an aging steel tank, the sacrificial anode rod that is supposed to corrode INSTEAD of the tank may be spent, letting the tank walls themselves rust into the stored water. First draws after a still week stir that sediment up.

Test the trend over the next day: run the hot water and see if it clears after a few minutes and stays clear with normal use. A one-morning event that clears and does not return is mostly stirred sediment. Brown that returns every morning, or deepens over weeks, says the anode is gone and the tank is consuming itself — at that point the question is the heater's age. Anode replacement can add years to a mid-life tank; a tank past ten or twelve years with rusty water is usually a replacement conversation, and both are plumber visits.

Two cautions. Do not drink or cook with discolored water until it runs clear, and if the COLD water ever joins in or the street's neighbors report the same, it stops being your heater and becomes a utility main issue — call them. But hot-only, after a still week, in an older tank: the heater is telling you its age. Believe it, and get the anode question answered while the tank is still a maintenance item rather than a flood.
My toilet tank has a puddle under it every morning, but the floor is dry during the day. Is the tank actually leaking, or could it be something else?

A puddle that appears overnight and vanishes by day has a strong innocent suspect: condensation. In humid weather, the tank fills with cold water after each flush; the porcelain sweats like a cold glass, and drips run down to the floor. Morning is peak time because overnight flushes fill the tank with the coldest water into the most humid air. A true leak, by contrast, usually shows some dampness whenever you check, and often leaves a mineral trail or a warped floor edge over time.

Separate them with two dry observations. First, the dry-and-watch test: before bed, dry the tank and floor completely with a towel. In the morning, run your hand over the tank's outside before checking the floor. A tank beaded with moisture all over, including high up where no fitting exists, is sweating. A single wet track running from one bolt or the supply connection is a leak with an address.

Second, the dye test separates internal from external: color the tank water; if color shows in the bowl, that is an internal flapper leak (a different problem, water bill rather than floor). For the floor puddle itself, lay a paper towel under the tank bolts and one under the supply line overnight — whichever is wet at dawn names the source: bolt gaskets, supply fitting, or neither (condensation).

Condensation fixes are ventilation, a mixing valve, or an insulated tank liner — comfort items. A bolt or fitting leak is a plumber-or-confident-DIY snug-down or gasket swap, water off first. And if the floor under it is soft or the puddle is growing, stop investigating and call: subfloors forgive neither leaks nor long delays.
The washing machine drain overflows the pipe it empties into, just for the first few seconds of the drain cycle. The sink next to it drains fine. What is happening in that pipe?

The standpipe — the vertical pipe the washer hose hooks into — is receiving water faster than it can swallow it, and the overflow at the start of the cycle is the giveaway shape. A washer's pump empties the tub in a powerful burst, much faster than a sink drains by gravity. If the standpipe or its trap carries a partial restriction — and laundry lines grow a famous one, a felted mat of lint, detergent sludge, and sock-adjacent debris — the burst overwhelms it in the first seconds until a head of water builds and forces the flow through.

The sink draining fine is your localization evidence: the shared drain beyond the laundry branch is clear, so the restriction sits in the standpipe's own run, between the opening and where it joins the larger line. This is branch logic, the same tree reasoning as any drain problem: what is slow names where it is slow.

Homeowner scope here is observation and one gentle tool: check that the washer hose is not shoved too far down the standpipe (it should hook in loosely, not sealed — an air gap matters), and look for lint buildup right at the trap entry. A small hand auger in the standpipe is a common DIY step. What you should NOT do is pour caustic drain cleaner down it — the overflow will happily splash it back, and it does nothing for a lint mat.

If the overflow grows, or water starts appearing at the washer's base instead, or the standpipe gurgles when other fixtures drain, the branch has company-wide problems and a plumber's auger earns its keep. Report the exact pattern: 'overflows for the first seconds of pump-out only, sink beside it fine.' That sentence is most of the diagnosis already.

It is 15 degrees out and the kitchen faucet — on an outside wall — has stopped running entirely. Every other faucet works. The pipes have not burst as far as I can tell. What do I do, and what do I not do?

You likely have a frozen section in that exterior-wall run, and the next few hours decide whether it stays a story or becomes a flood. The single-fixture, coldest-wall, coldest-night pattern is the classic signature: the pipe froze at its most exposed point, and ice is now corking it.

Do these things. Open the kitchen faucet and leave it open — as ice melts, the water needs somewhere to go, and a closed faucet lets pressure build between the ice and the tap. Open the cabinet doors under the sink so warm room air reaches the pipes. Warm the area gently: a space heater aimed at the cabinet from a safe distance, or a hair dryer on the exposed pipe under the sink if you can reach it. Keep the rest of the house warm. And locate your main shutoff NOW, before anything thaws, so if a split reveals itself you can kill the water in seconds.

Do NOT use a torch, heat gun on high, or any open flame on a pipe — that is how frozen pipes become house fires, and it can also boil water inside the pipe and burst it. Do not leave the house with a frozen pipe unattended. Do not assume no burst: ice often plugs its own split, and the leak only announces itself at thaw. Watch the meter and the cabinet as flow returns; if water appears anywhere it should not, main shutoff first, then the plumber.

Afterward, the prevention list writes itself: insulation on that wall run, cabinet doors open on the coldest nights, and a pencil-thin trickle from that faucet when temperatures dive — moving water resists freezing. Tonight, though: faucet open, gentle heat, shutoff located, eyes on it.
I just walked into my kitchen and I can smell gas near the stove. Nobody is cooking. What exactly should I do?

Leave. That is the whole first step, and it outranks everything else. Gas odor in a house is not a diagnosis problem; it is an evacuation problem. The rotten-egg smell is an additive put there precisely so you will act on it, and the correct action is to get everyone — people and pets — out of the house now.

While leaving, obey three don'ts, because ordinary actions make sparks: do not flip light switches or any electrical switch on or off, do not use a phone or flashlight inside the house, and do not try to find the leak, open windows on a tour of the house, or turn the stove knobs to check them. If a burner knob is obviously on and you pass it on your way out, one motion to off is fine — but do not stop to investigate, sniff around the oven, or light anything to test it. Every second inside is exposure to a mixture that only needs one spark.

From outside — a neighbor's yard, the sidewalk, well away from the house — call your gas utility's emergency line or 911. They will tell you not to re-enter, and they will come with detectors and shut the gas off at the meter, which is their job and their equipment, never yours. Do not go back in for belongings, and do not air the house out yourself and declare it fine; gas can pool in low spots and linger. The utility will clear the house formally before anyone re-enters.

Later, after the all-clear, there will be time to learn whether it was an unlit burner, a failing flex line, or something else, and a licensed plumber or the utility will handle that part. Right now the only correct sentence is the one you act on: smell gas, get out, call from outside.

My gas water heater's pilot light keeps going out. I relight it following the instructions printed on the tank and it stays lit for a day or two, then dies again. Is relighting it repeatedly a problem?

Relighting it once or twice by the printed instructions is normal homeowner life. A pilot that will not STAY lit for more than a day or two is a symptom with a short list of causes, and continuing to relight it for weeks is where the line sits — not because relighting is dangerous in itself, but because you are masking a part that is failing by design.

The pilot's guardian is the thermocouple: a small probe sitting in the pilot flame that generates a tiny voltage while hot, and that voltage is what holds the gas valve open to the pilot. No flame, no voltage, valve closes — that is the safety working. When a thermocouple ages, its output sags: the flame lights, things warm up, but the marginal voltage drops out hours or days later and the valve closes. That intermittent pattern — lights fine, dies in a day or two — is the thermocouple's classic farewell. The alternatives are a pilot flame that is weak or dirty (a small, lazy, yellow-ish flame instead of a crisp blue one enveloping the probe — observe it through the sight glass without opening anything), or drafts and venting problems disturbing the flame.

Your observation homework: note the flame's color and size when lit, whether outages correlate with windy days (venting) or with the furnace running (shared flue effects), and how long it stays lit each cycle. Then the call: thermocouple replacement and burner cleaning involve the gas train and burner assembly — licensed plumber or HVAC territory, not a homeowner repair, because gas connections must be leak-checked afterward.

One hard stop inside all of this: if you ever smell gas around the heater beyond the brief moment of relighting, stop, leave, and call the utility from outside. A tired thermocouple is a nuisance; a gas smell is an evacuation. Know which problem you have.
I have no hot water at all — the tap runs lukewarm at best, forever, no matter how long I wait. My electric heater is only six years old. My neighbor's theory is a burned-out element. Is he right?

Half right — probably AN element, but your symptom names WHICH one, and it is not the one people guess. In an electric tank, the upper element does the first and most important work: it heats the top of the tank to full temperature, and only when the upper thermostat is satisfied does control pass to the lower element to heat the rest. The upper element is the gatekeeper.

Now read your symptom through that design. Endless lukewarm, never hot: the upper element (or its thermostat) has failed. The lower element may be perfectly healthy, but it never gets its turn, because the upper thermostat never sees 'hot enough' to hand over. What little warmth you get is incidental. Contrast with the opposite failure — lower element dead — where showers START properly hot and die early. The two element failures produce opposite symptoms, and yours is the upper's signature.

Six years is young for a tank but a normal lifespan for an element in hard water, so the age does not argue against it.

The boundary, stated plainly: verifying this means testing elements and thermostats at line voltage inside the heater's access panels. That is electrician or plumber work. Your neighborly debate ends with the symptom logic, and your call to the pro should carry it: 'endless lukewarm, never hot — I believe the upper element or its thermostat.' Expect them to test both elements and both thermostats while they are in there, because at six years the marginal cost of checking everything beats a second visit. And if both elements test fine, the next suspect is a thermostat set wrong or failed — same visit, same tools, same boundary.
My water heater makes a rumbling, popping sound like popcorn while it heats. It has done it for months and the water is fine. Am I ignoring something I should not?

You are hearing sediment — and yes, it is worth acting on, though it is a maintenance clock, not an emergency alarm. Here is the mechanism. Minerals precipitate out of heated water and settle on the tank's floor as a rocky layer. In a gas heater, burner heat must pass through that layer; pockets of water trapped under and within the sediment flash to steam, and the pops and rumbles are those steam bubbles collapsing. In an electric heater the same layer blankets the lower element and makes it cook itself.

The costs of ignoring it compound quietly: the heater burns extra fuel heating rock before water, the tank floor overheats and its lining degrades faster, the lower element's life shortens, and in the endgame the sediment can reach the drain valve and the hot outlet. Rumbling that has run for months is the middle chapters of that story, not the last one — you have time, but the meter is running.

The remedy is flushing the tank through its drain valve until the water runs clear — a real maintenance procedure involving hot water, a hose, and the heater's controls. Many homeowners do it; if you are not fully confident with the steps for your fuel type (gas heaters need the burner managed correctly, electrics must never have elements energized in a drained tank — an element fired in air burns out in seconds), this is an inexpensive plumber visit, and annual flushing after that keeps the layer from rebuilding. Hand over the symptom in one sentence: 'rumbling during heat cycles for months.' Also note the tank's age: past ten or twelve years, a plumber may fairly ask whether flushing money belongs in a tank near replacement — that judgment call is exactly what you are paying them for.
