The fix is choreography or geography: run the two big loads in sequence, or move one to an outlet on the kitchen's OTHER circuit — most kitchens have two small-appliance circuits by design; your breaker map tells you which outlets belong to which.

One warning that belongs in every version of this conversation: the correct response to this arithmetic is never a bigger breaker and never a defeated one. The 20 A limit is the wire's limit. The math is the math, and the breaker is just the part of the house that refuses to let you argue with it.
My dishwasher has started leaving the dishes gritty and the water at the kitchen tap takes longer to get hot than it used to. Both started around the same month. One problem or two?

Run the shared-pathway test: these two symptoms share the hot water supply, so unlike most same-month pairs, they may genuinely be one problem wearing two aprons. A dishwasher that leaves grit is often a dishwasher receiving water that is not hot enough (it relies on incoming heat for its first fill and for dissolving detergent) or water carrying sediment that redeposits on dishes. A tap that is slower to deliver heat points back at the heater or the hot line, not at the tap.

Interrogate the water heater with your senses and a thermometer. At the tap nearest the heater, after a minute's run, what is the actual temperature? If it has sagged from, say, 125°F toward 110°F, everything downstream feels it: showers get shorter tempers, dishwashers underperform. Then listen to the heater during a heating cycle — rumbling and popping means a sediment blanket, which both insulates the water from the burner or element (slower recovery, lower effective temperature) and sheds grit into the hot lines (your dishes' new texture). One mechanism, both symptoms: that is a satisfying unification.

The alternative unifier lives at the dishwasher itself — a clogged inlet screen or spray arms — but that explains gritty dishes only, not the tap's slower heat, so it fails the shared test unless the tap complaint has a separate cause like a failing cartridge mixing cold in. Check the tap temperature first: it is the witness that decides between 'the heater is aging into sediment' and 'two appliances aging independently.'

If the heater is the story, the remedy conversation is the sediment one — flushing, anode check, age judgment — with a plumber, and your two-symptom observation, dated to the same month, is the brief that gets them there directly. Same-month is a clue, never a conclusion; the shared pathway is what promotes it.
My well pump seems to cycle on and off every few minutes even when nobody is using water. My neighbor with a well says that is bad for the pump. What is the system doing?

Your neighbor is right, and the pattern has a name: short cycling. A well system stores pressurized water in a pressure tank — water on one side of a bladder, compressed air on the other. The pump fills the tank until pressure peaks (often 50 or 60 psi), then rests while the house draws the tank down to the cut-in pressure (30 or 40 psi). A healthy tank gives the pump long rests and long runs. Cycling every few minutes with no water being used means the pressure is draining away almost as fast as the pump restores it — the system's stored buffer is gone or leaking.

Two families of causes, and one observation separates them. First: is water actually leaving? Run the house-side check — no fixtures running, watch for a toilet leak (dye test) or any of the silent-loss suspects; a real leak downstream makes the pump replace lost water forever. Second, and more likely with your exact symptom: the pressure tank's bladder has failed or its air charge is lost — the tank is waterlogged, just like a failed expansion tank on a water heater, so it stores almost nothing. The pump fills the pipes to cut-off in seconds, a small draw drops pressure instantly, and the pump restarts. Each start is the hardest moment in a pump's life; thousands of extra starts a week is how pumps die young.

Homeowner scope: observe the cycle timing (log it: run time, rest time), dye-test the toilets, and confirm no irrigation or hose is sipping. The tank and switch work itself — checking the air charge requires draining the system and gauging the tank's Schrader valve at zero water pressure, and pump controls carry line voltage — belongs to a well or plumbing professional. Your log is the gift: 'cycles every three minutes, no water use, toilets dye-clean' tells them to bring a pressure tank, not a fishing license. And do not let it run like this for months while you decide — the pump is spending its life to tell you this.

The light in my stairwell is controlled by switches at the top and bottom. It works, but lately I sometimes flip a switch and nothing happens — I flip it again and it works. Is the switch wearing out?

Possibly, but first make sure the system is not fooling you — three-way switches have no ON or OFF position printed for a reason: each switch simply connects the common to one of two travelers, and the light's state depends on BOTH switches' positions. With two switches there are four combinations; the light is on in two of them. Flipping one switch always changes the state IF the other switch's position completes or breaks the path in the ordinary way — and this is where your symptom gets interesting, because 'flip once, nothing; flip again, works' is NOT something a healthy three-way pair can do. In a healthy pair, every single flip toggles the light, always. A flip that does nothing means the contact inside one switch is failing to make or break connection intermittently — a worn or dirty contact, exactly your suspicion, or a loose terminal making contact only when the mechanism lands firmly.

Localize which switch: use the other switch to set the light on, then work the suspect switch slowly several times, noting whether its action feels gritty, loose, or different from its partner. A switch that feels vague and behaves vaguely is confessing. Also note whether the dead flips correlate with one particular switch or happen at both ends — both ends misbehaving suggests the problem is not two switches dying in duet but something shared, which changes the brief.

The boundary: replacing a three-way switch means three or four wires in a box and a real chance of creating the classic both-switches-must-be-up puzzle if travelers and common get crossed — take the photograph-first rule seriously if this is ever DIY'd by a confident person, and treat it as an electrician job by default. What you report: 'three-way pair, intermittent no-op flips at the bottom switch, gritty feel.' A failing switch contact does not heal, and one that arcs a little more each month earns its replacement sooner rather than later.
I want to know if my house's water pressure is in a healthy range and whether it changes during the day. Can I measure that myself, and what numbers should I expect?

Yes — this is one of the best homeowner measurements there is, and the tool is a simple pressure gauge that threads onto a hose bib or laundry tap, costing less than a pizza. No pipes opened, nothing disassembled: screw it on, open the tap fully, read the needle.

Take two kinds of readings. Static pressure: all water use in the house stopped, gauge tap open — this is the pressure the street or your PRV delivers at rest. Healthy residential range is roughly 40 to 80 psi; many homes sit at 50 to 65. Above 80 psi is a finding: it stresses every valve, hose, and appliance in the house, worsens water hammer, and shortens the life of toilet fill valves and washing machine hoses — a pressure-reducing valve conversation for a plumber. Below 40 explains a houseful of apologetic showers.

Then the dynamic story: read the gauge while a shower and a flush run elsewhere. A drop of 10 to 20 psi under demand is normal; a collapse of 30 or more suggests a restriction (a failing PRV, a partly closed main, corroded supply piping) between the street and you. And repeat the static reading at a few times of day — municipal pressure often rises at night when the neighborhood sleeps, and a house at 70 psi by day can sit at 95 at 3 a.m.; that night peak is what your plumbing actually lives with, and it reframes several other diagnoses.

Log all of it in the house book: static day, static night, dynamic under load. Those three numbers become the baseline every future pressure complaint gets compared against, and they are the first thing a plumber asks for in any pressure investigation. You will have measured them for the price of lunch, without opening a single fitting — the cost-of-information ladder working exactly as designed.

Give me a complete diagnostic plan for this: a rental duplex I manage has rising water bills in ONE unit, occasional sewage smell in that unit's bathroom, and the tenant reports the tub drains slowly 'sometimes.' Three vague symptoms. Where do I start and in what order?

Treat this as three symptoms that may share one root, and sequence your investigation by information value per dollar — cheapest and most discriminating tests first, and nothing invasive until the cheap tests have spoken.

Step one, quantify the water loss, because 'rising bills' is currently an adjective. Compare the unit's billed usage month over month (the utility's numbers, not the tenant's impression), then run the meter test on that unit: no water use for two hours, meter read before and after. This tells you whether water is being lost continuously (supply-side leak or running toilet — the champions of silent loss) and at what rate. A rate like 3 gallons an hour reframes everything downstream.

Step two, the toilets, because statistics demand it: dye-test every toilet in the unit. A leaking flapper explains rising bills completely and costs almost nothing to confirm or exclude.

Step three, connect or separate the drain symptoms. Sewage smell plus an intermittently slow tub is a different family — drainage and venting, not supply. The word 'sometimes' is the tell: a tub that is slow only when other fixtures discharge (washer pump-out, the other unit's usage if lines are shared) suggests a partially restricted or poorly vented shared branch, where smell escapes through the tub's trap when the line pressurizes — the same mechanism as gurgling. Map it with the tenant's help: slow tub WHEN — after laundry, during the neighbor unit's showers, randomly? And check whether the smell tracks those same moments.

Step four, synthesize before spending. If the meter test shows continuous loss and the dye test finds it, the bills are solved and the drain pair is a separate, second problem — schedule a plumber for the drain with your timing map in hand. If the meter is still and toilets are clean, the 'rising bill' may be billing-period or occupancy noise, and the drain problem becomes the main event — still plumber territory, because shared duplex lines and vent stacks are not a landlord's DIY.

Throughout, the management discipline: everything in writing to the tenant, dates on every test, and habitability symptoms (sewage smell is one) get professional response on a prompt clock regardless of diagnostic elegance — in most jurisdictions that is law, not courtesy. Order of operations: measure, test the cheap champions, map the intermittent symptom against time, then buy exactly the professional visit the evidence describes. That sequence is the whole method — evidence before expenditure, and the vague becomes specific one cheap test at a time.
